terms.comment: Morgan–Owens’s word, from the modern languages; the cooking species is Cymbopogon citratus.

terms.gloss: an aromatic rush used to flavour wine, a near kin of lemongrass
evidence: Cato Agr. 105: Schoenum et calamum in pīlā contunditō
terms.comment: Cato’s and Columella’s sweet rush, pounded in a mortar and put into wine. Lewis & Short says only “a rush, of an aromatic kind”; botanists take it for camel grass, of the same genus as lemongrass. Use it of lemongrass only knowingly.

phrases.latin: Citrōnellam in jūs addam; suāviter olet.
phrases.english: I’ll put lemongrass in the broth; it smells lovely.
Do you want to pound the lemongrass? Here’s the pestle.

phrases.latin: Schoenum et calamum in pīlā contunditō, quod satis siet, sextārium ūnum eōdem in dōlium īnfunditō, ut odōrātum siet.
phrases.english: Pound sweet rush and sweet flag in a mortar, as much as is enough, and pour one sextarius into the same jar, so that it may be fragrant.

sources: Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. lemon grass.
